title: Stanford's Code in Place Info Session with Mehran Sahami
transcriptText:
SPEAKER: Today, we are joined by
Mehran Sahami, who many of you
already know from his
work in computer science.
Mehran has played a key
role in shaping the program
and making thousands of
students learn programming
in a very engaging way.
I won't go deep
into his background
since he'll be introducing
himself shortly,
but we are really lucky to
have him here with us today.
And with that, I will
hand it off to him.
MEHRAN SAHAMI: Thanks very much.
Hi, everyone.
Thanks for joining us.
And wherever and
whatever time you're
in, good morning, good
afternoon, good evening,
or good night.
But we're very happy
you joined us here.
I want to spend a
little bit of time
telling you about Code in
Place and give you information.
Whether you're interested in
being a student or a section
leader, give you an
overview of the class.
And so to do that,
what I'm going to do
is start by sharing
some slides with you.
We'll go through a few things.
And then we'll answer lots
of questions at the end
if there's any questions.
So, to get started.
I'm going to share
my screen with you.
Hopefully, you can
see some slides now,
talking about Code in Place.
And Code in Place
is really a program
that was put together by
my colleague, Chris Piech.
And I played some role in
that, and we teach it together.
And what I want to do is spend
a little bit of time telling you
what Code in Place is,
why it's a unique program
and give you some general
logistics for the program
so you can see what
are the kinds of things
you would do in it and how
you would get involved.
And give you, hopefully,
some encouragement
to start something
beautiful by getting
involved in the program, which
is really what we'd love to see.
So to tell you a little bit
about myself, as you heard,
my name is Mehran Sahami.
I was actually born in
Iran, grew up in San
Diego, California,
in the United States.
And many years ago,
actually, was a student
at Stanford for my bachelor's,
master's, and eventually
PhD in machine learning.
I like to say before
machine learning was cool.
Now it seems like
machine learning
and artificial
intelligence are all over.
But many years ago,
that was not the case.
And I actually
spent about 10 years
in industry, most of that
time at a little company
called Google that you
might have heard of,
before I came back to Stanford,
about 20 years ago now,
to be a professor.
And the reason I came
back to be a professor
is because I really
loved teaching.
And so Code in Place is
just a program that's
very near and dear to my heart.
The person who had
done most of the work,
actually, in starting Code in
Place, one of my colleagues
whose office is actually right
next door to mine at Stanford,
is Chris Piech, who is just
a wonderful human being.
Chris grew up in
Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur.
He came to Stanford
as an undergraduate.
Stayed for graduate
school, much like I did.
Now he's a professor
at Stanford,
is involved in running
a research lab that
does lots of research
in education,
and really is the heart
and soul of Code in Place
and just an amazing,
amazing human being.
And one of the things I
really love about Chris
is his humanity.
Not only is he a great computer
scientist, a great technologist,
but he just really
cares about people,
and he really cares about making
a difference in the world.
And he actually-- this
is him with his daughter.
He actually just
had another baby.
Or actually, his wife
just had another baby.
So that's why he's not
here with me right now.
Importantly, he's helping
take care of the baby.
But just an amazing person,
and someone that you'll
actually see teaching classes
along with me in Code in Place.
But in order to teach a class
the size of Code in Place,
it takes a whole
bunch of people.
It's not just the two of us.
So there's a wonderful
leadership team
for the whole
program that we do.
Just lots of people
who've been involved
in various aspects
of the program,
helping to build things, helping
to create educational materials,
helping to teach.
And I just want to
acknowledge that whole team,
because they've
done a lot of stuff,
and it's just an
amazing group of people.
And every year, we also have
a group of head teaching
assistants that help train the
section leaders for the program.
You'll find out who section
leaders are in just a second.
So I wanted to show you
their pictures as well.
Just a great group
of people over time
who've helped to
train section leaders,
help to create parts
of the program.
Many of these folks are going
to be working with us this time
around.
This is our sixth version
of doing Code in Place.
And they just do
really amazing things.
So I want to tell you a
little bit of a story.
So it's gather around the fire.
Here's a little
story for you that
has to do with how
Code in Place started.
So about 6 years
ago, Chris and I
were about to teach
CS106A, which is Stanford's
introductory programming class.
And then suddenly
the world changed.
And if you remember what
happened about 6 years ago,
the coronavirus pandemic hit.
And we were sitting
there wondering,
what can we do to help?
Because during this
time, there was not only
just a pandemic of
disease going around,
but there was also a
pandemic of loneliness.
Many people were stuck at home.
They were sheltering in place.
There was also a pandemic
of education inequality,
because many people were
not actually receiving
education in school.
And Chris and I thought,
what could we do?
So he actually called me up and
we were having a conversation.
And we thought, well,
we're not medical doctors,
so we can't be out in the
field, but maybe we can actually
do something around
education, because if people
are stuck at home, this might
be an opportunity for them
to be able to learn.
And if you remember
at the time, there
was a phrase called shelter in
place, where they were telling
people to stay at home unless
it was essential for them
to come into work.
And we thought, well, if
people are sheltering in place,
maybe we could take this as an
opportunity to teach them how
to Code in Place, which is
where the name of the program
actually comes from.
And the question
that we wanted to ask
by putting this program together
was, how can we scale access
to human-centric
computer science
education for a community
service project?
Is there a way that
we can make education
available to a large number of
students all around the world
to be able to learn
something, maybe to even have
a potential career change as
the pandemic was going on?
And when we thought
about this, we
thought, if you have a
large number of students,
what's really the
secret sauce that
makes this work at Stanford?
Because at Stanford,
we teach a few hundred
students every quarter
this material in a class
called CS106A.
What's the secret
sauce of that class,
which is our introductory
computer science class?
It was the class
that Chris and I
were about to teach about
6 years ago together.
And the way we do
it at Stanford is
we have a group of people
called section leaders.
They are people who meet with
small cohorts of students,
about 10 students to
every section leader,
and they meet with
them every week
to be able to provide more
personalized instruction,
provide a level
of accountability
to check in to make sure
the students are doing OK.
And the students
feel, because there's
this person who's working
with them that closely, they
feel more likely to want to
continue on with the class
and work through things.
So what we do is
we take the class
and we break it up
into smaller groups
that we refer to as sections.
And for each of these
groups of students,
we provide a section leader,
who is the person who
meets with these students once
every week to go over materials,
to help them with
individualized instruction
if they need more
personalization.
And really, just to
provide that level
of closer interaction,
which we think
is really key, that
human connection,
to help people
really learn and get
through the educational process.
And the beautiful thing is
the most recent iteration,
for example, we had over 1,600
section leaders help us with
the class, which means we can
scale the class to enormous
proportions.
And really, when we think about
where these section leaders come
from, and this idea that we
could have this many section
leaders in a class comes
from a particular notion,
which is that human potential
is drastically underutilized
when we think about education.
In some ways, the
magnitude of people
who actually want
to teach is roughly
proportional to the magnitude
of people who want to learn.
And if we think about
teaching as being itself
a learning process, when you
want to teach someone else,
you're learning more
from that yourself.
That's certainly true for me
as a professor and the time
I've spent as an educator.
And the teaching can
actually be really joyful.
It helps create
connections between people.
It helps people understand that
we're all in this together,
and we can help
each other doing it,
and it's just a
wonderful experience.
So if you can harness
that potential of people
who want to teach and create
a structure in which they can
teach many other people, then
we can create essentially
the foundation for what
we call Code in Place.
And to give you a
sense of how much we've
scaled that potential
over time, to date,
we've run five iterations
of Code in Place.
We're about to start the
sixth one, which is why we're
doing this information session.
And we've taught over 60,000
students around the world how
to code with the help of
over 5,500 section leaders,
who've been teaching
Stanford's CS106A materials,
about half to
two-thirds of the class,
of the actual class
we teach at Stanford.
And they teach it in
the-- for the students,
it's completely free for
students around the world.
And the students come from
pretty much everywhere
in the world.
So if you look at
where they come from,
there's over 150 countries that
have been represented in Code
in Place over the years.
We have a broad gender
distribution of students.
We have a very broad age
distribution of students.
And one of the things that's
actually lovely to see
is that you're never
too old to learn.
So sometimes people
worry, is it too late
for me to learn something new?
Especially for computer science,
it's never too late to learn.
So if you're worried
about that, you
don't need to worry about it.
The way we like to think about
this is our learning goal
is we want to really
inspire students to want
to continue learning to code.
Code in Place is a great start.
We teach a lot of programming.
We make people build
some interesting projects
that they really enjoy.
And the thing is
that they-- part
of the goal of
having the section
leaders from the class
that's having a class that's
really welcoming and supportive,
we'll have a lot of support
in there, as you'll find out,
is we want to give people
a new skill, but we
also want to motivate
them to complete the class.
And so if you look at the
completion rates of Code
in Place over the years,
it's really quite astounding.
If you consider most massive
open online classes, sometimes
referred to as MOOCs,
their completion rates
are down, usually in the
single-digit percentages.
Usually around 5%, sometimes
as low as things like 1% or 2%.
The completion rate
for Code in Place
is usually between 50% and 60%.
That's more than 10
times the completion rate
for traditional online classes.
Why is that?
It's because we harness
the secret sauce, which
is the power of section leaders
to create that human connection,
to motivate people to want
to continue on in the class.
And we've seen this
happen year after year
that we teach Code in Place.
It's the structure that
really makes a difference.
So let's spend a
little bit of time
talking about the structure
of the class itself.
What happens in Code in Place?
Well, we can think
about different roles
that you might be interested
in for Code in Place.
If you're a section
leader, or if you're
thinking about being a section
leader for the class, which
is the person who's
actually going to have help
teach a cohort of 10 students,
or close to that number,
in the class.
The things we have are,
first, a welcome meeting,
where we have all
the section leaders
get together to learn
more about what's
going on behind the
scenes in Code in Place
and learn more about the role
of being a section leader.
Then we have two live
practice sections
that you would go
to to just give you
more familiarity with
how sections work
and to help you
with your teaching.
And then, during the
course of Code in Place,
it's a 6-week program, you will
teach six sections to students.
So that's the responsibilities
of section leaders.
Really, we bring you
into our program.
We provide some training
on the teaching side,
and to go over materials
and to see what it's
like to teach your sections.
And then we have you actually
teach sections to students.
And it's just a
lovely experience.
As I mentioned, we've
had thousands of people
be section leaders
for the program.
And if you're
thinking about it, I'd
really encourage you to apply.
It's just a
fantastic experience.
Now, if you're thinking about
being a student for Code
in Place, you might wonder,
what's the background?
What's the prerequisite
that I actually
need to take this class?
Well, here's the
interesting thing.
If you can tell whether or
not that computer I just
showed you is on or
off and compare it
to the screen next to it to
determine if that computer is
on or off, that's
pretty much all you need
to be able to do Code in Place.
I mean, realistically, you
need to be able to get around
the computer.
You need to know how to use a
mouse and what a web browser is.
But you know what?
If you're on this
webinar right now,
you already have
those prerequisites,
because you figured
out a way to be here.
So you pretty much, if you're
considering being a student,
you have the prerequisites
to be in Code in Place.
Really, what we're going to
teach you is from the ground up,
we assume no previous
programming knowledge.
From the ground up, we're going
to teach you how to program
and how to build some
pretty amazing things.
The language we use in CS106A is
the programming language Python.
That's the same language
we use in Code in Place.
And you might say, why do
we actually use Python?
Well, if you look at
this little chart,
there's a lot of
stuff going on, but it
measures the popularity of
different programming languages.
And if you look at the
far right of the chart,
you might see a light
blue line that's
higher than all the other lines.
That's the line for Python.
So that's why we teach it.
It's the language
that's actually
used very much in industry.
It's used for
artificial intelligence.
It's used to program a lot
of things, including things
like data understanding and data
simulations for data science,
for programming games.
It has lots and lots
of applications.
And so that's part
of the reason why
we're going to use
it in Code in Place,
because it's a real
programming language.
Now what do students do?
We have a whole
website set up for you
that has structure around
the kinds of things
that we provide for you.
So let me go through
some of the things
that we provide
in Code in Place.
There are videos which
are student lessons.
And so, every week
there's a new set
of videos that will be released.
This is where you will get your
instruction for Code in Place.
Many of these videos
mirror the actual classes
we have at Stanford.
So the idea is to give you
high-quality instruction
every week with
new materials that
get released to you to go over.
Perhaps most importantly,
in addition to the videos,
you get what we like to
refer to as the main content
of the class, every
week you'll be meeting
in a section for 50 minutes.
That's a live section on
Zoom with a section leader,
and it will give you a
chance to ask questions,
to go over materials, to really
feel engaged and involved
in the class in a
meaningful way, where
you'll be working with
a cohort of people
and you can all learn together.
And that's really
part of the beauty.
It's not just watching
a set of videos,
it's actually interacting
with other people
to learn the material
in more detail.
And if you have questions, to
get those questions answered.
So you can continue
your learning process
all the way through the class.
Now, along the way, there's
also additional materials
besides the videos of the
content and the sections
that we provide.
There's online readings
that we give you
that have more material that
you can also use as a reference
as you're going through
and learning everything.
We have an online
environment for programming.
And in that online environment,
we have lots of work examples,
examples of actual programs,
examples of problems
that you can do, so
that that way, you
can build your
skills more and more.
We give you lots
of opportunities
to be able to practice and to
engage with these problems.
All you need is a web browser.
So you don't even need to
worry about downloading
a bunch of software to your own
computer, other than the things
to be able to do the video
conferencing for your section.
But in terms of the actual
programming environment,
that's all done
online, and we give you
lots of examples
and lots of support.
There's also a discussion
forum, and we've
built this discussion forum to
be most helpful to students.
It's a place where
you can ask questions.
Lots of people are
helping each other.
The section leaders
show up to help
students in the discussion
forum, to help answer questions.
Students answer questions
for other students.
It's just a fun,
vibrant community
of people who are really engaged
in helping each other learn.
And we love that.
And there are times
Chris and I will also
get on that discussion forum.
The head TAs will be there.
And it's just a great place to
be able to use as reference.
And to ask questions to
get more answers to things.
And as I mentioned
before, we have an amazing
what I refer to as an integrated
development environment, or IDE
is sometimes the acronym
that's used in industry,
which is the place where you
can do all your programming.
And so, it's kind of a
place where you can come,
you can work on your
programming problems.
And as I mentioned, we
also have examples there.
So you can try things to
help you build up your skills
as you continue to
do work in the class.
So the course has a
particular rhythm to it.
Every week there'll
be some tasks
that you will complete as a
student that will teach you
more and more programming.
There will be a section that you
will have at a particular time.
If you're a section leader,
you'll be teaching that section.
If you're a student, you'll
be in the class as a student.
And so we give you an
overview of each week.
And every week we
have a little session
that tells you what's
going on that week.
And during the
plan of the course.
What we do is we start with
a very simple language called
Karel the Robot.
And it's a language
that was actually
developed by someone at
Stanford many years ago as a way
to introduce students
to programming
in a very straightforward
and very simple way.
It's also a language
we use at Stanford.
So you're getting the
same Stanford experience
as the students here to get
that gentle introduction
to programming from Karel.
That's for the first
week of the class.
And then, from there, we
transition into Python.
And when we learn Python,
you'll learn all the basics
of programming in Python.
We'll also do some
neat things where
you'll learn about how to do
graphics in Python, animations,
and then also be
able to analyze data.
So there's lots of skills
you'll learn in the class that
will give you opportunities
to apply programming
in lots of ways, not only in
the class but after the class
as well.
And potentially continue
your learning process.
One of the things
that you'll find out
along the way is when
we teach you Karel,
you might be
wondering, why are you
teaching me this
different language?
Here's a little secret.
Karel is actually Python.
So there are certain
things about Karel
that look like a little robot
moving around the screen
to help you do some initial
learning about computing.
But in fact, everything that
you're programming in Karel
is actually in Python.
So when we switch
over to Python,
all that stuff that you learned
in Karel applies directly.
So you've been learning
Python the whole time.
We just make it a
little bit easier
at the beginning with
this little robot
called Karel that
we teach you about.
And after that, we unleash
you on full Python.
And we'll have you
write some programs
along the way as
part of the class,
including a program called
KHAN-sole Academy, which
is a lot of fun.
It's actually a program that
does little quizzes to help
teach people how to learn
different kinds of things,
like math.
And so, it's kind of fun,
because as a student,
you'll be writing
programs that are actually
teaching other people how to
do certain kinds of things.
We think of teaching as
just this large community
of students.
And as a learner,
you're still a teacher.
The other fun things
that we do that
involve graphics and animation,
like programming games.
And you'll learn how to draw
stuff on the screen in Python.
And the drawings
actually show up
in our little
development environment
that you'll be using.
And also thinking
about how to be
able to animate various kinds
of things or use programs
to generate pictures that
are just really neat.
And at the end, we have
a programming challenge
that allows you to
show your creativity,
to be able to think about
what something that you're
interested in
programming, and then
build that with what
you've learned in the class
so that you can show us how
much stuff you've learned
and in what ways that you want
to apply that in programming.
And that provides a little
more personalized way
of being able to apply things
that you've done in the class
to really build something
that you're happy with
and you're happy to
show other people.
Now, in terms of the
topics of the course,
if you're deciding to
potentially be a student
or you're thinking about being a
section leader, as I mentioned,
there's kind of a 6-week
main course itself.
There's, at the end,
we talk about how
you can continue your learning
and your final project.
But we go over lots
of things, like we
talk about Karel for actually
the first 2 weeks of the class.
We talk about the
basics of Python,
using just a text console is the
way we like to think about it.
And then we move into graphics.
And along the way we
learn some different sorts
of what are referred to
as data structures, which
are different ways
in a program that you
can keep track of information.
If you're thinking about
being a section leader,
some of the data structures
that we talk about
are lists and dictionaries.
The graphics library
that we talk about
is a pretty straightforward
graphics library.
So even if you
haven't had experience
with graphics in
the past in Python,
but you are familiar
with programming,
you can still be a section
leader for the course,
and it'll be very easy for you
to learn the graphics stuff.
If you're thinking
about being a student,
we'll teach you
everything from the basics
from the very beginning, so you
don't need to-- as I mentioned,
you don't need to have any
prerequisite for the class.
It's just a joyful experience.
And so when we think about
some of the course topics,
there's lots of things
that we cover in the class.
For people who are
familiar with programming,
the idea is we
get people started
with a warm-up assignment.
We have them think
about how to build up
from that warm-up to do
more challenging problems.
And then there's the
assignment for that week, which
might be a problem or a set of
problems that they actually do.
It's just a wonderful thing.
And in terms of
those course topics,
too, one of the things that we
also want students to really
be able to engage
with is there's
a whole cadence of materials
to be able to go through,
and you can always refer back
to earlier things in the course.
So if there's ever a time you
feel unsure about something that
came before, you can
go through and be
able to reference
to prior things.
So what are some of the
course values that we have?
Well, part of it
is, as I mentioned,
we want to teach the
art of computer science.
And there's really a science
behind computer science.
It's not just about learning
a programming language,
but it's actually teaching
software engineering principles.
And so we not only teach
you how to program,
but we teach you how to
be a good programmer.
And so there are certain
principles like abstraction,
decomposition, and modularity.
I won't go into a
lot of detail there.
But at a high level,
it's the thinking,
the notion of thinking about
how to take a big problem
and break it up
into smaller pieces,
and then be able to solve
those smaller pieces
and combine them together
to solve a bigger problem.
And the analogy I
like to use with this
is that many
people, for example,
know how to use a
toaster to toast bread,
but most people don't know
how to build a toaster.
That's the notion
of abstraction.
Sometimes you can use
something without knowing
how to build it yourself.
And in programming, it
turns out that there's
lots of things that were
already built by other people.
So you don't need to build them
yourselves, but you can actually
use those things as
part of the programs
you write to be able to do even
better kinds of things, even
cooler kinds of programs.
And so that's where
we think about how
to understand those principles
in programming so you
can write just neater programs.
And those are things we'll cover
as we go through the class.
One of the other values we
have in the class that's
very important to us is to make
sure that everyone in the class
is successful.
Everyone is welcome
in the class.
All kinds of backgrounds,
all kinds of different levels
of education.
We really want to make
computing and programming
available to anyone who's
interested in doing it.
We want you to find real
intellectual joy in what you're
doing.
And so we try to make
teaching a joyful process.
We have fun doing it.
Sometimes we tell
jokes, sometimes
we do different kinds
of demonstrations.
And one of the
things we really care
about, why did we even create
Code in Place to begin with,
is we think kindness
is really important.
And that's not just kindness
from the course staff to you.
It's kindness for
all the students
and section leaders in
the class to each other.
We want to create a community
where everyone feels welcome,
where everyone feels valued.
And that's part of
the real principles
and underlying
values of the class.
And a notion of gratitude.
Like, for us, it's so important
and it's so meaningful
that we get so many people
from around the world who
want to be teachers
or section leaders
or who want to try something new
by taking a programming class.
We have a huge amount
of gratitude for that.
And just for joining
